deep_dive.title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
deep_dive.abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.

deep_dive.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
deep_dive.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

deep_dive.title: Large Multimodal Models for Direct Robot Control: GPT-6 as a Beginning
deep_dive.abstract: Recent advances in visuospatial understanding and agentic reasoning enable direct robotic manipulation with general-purpose multimodal models, but their embodied capabilities remain poorly understood. This paper systematically evaluate GPT-6 Astra for closed-loop robotic manipulation using a lightweight agent execution framework. We first probe three fundamental embodied capabilities-depth perception, embodied in-context learning, and tactile understanding-and demonstrate that the model can exploit depth information, acquire simple manipulation strategies from contextual demonstrations, and use tactile feedback to correct its actions. We then evaluate GPT-6 Astra across five established manipulation benchmarks along six capability dimensions. Despite competitive performance on several benchmarks-26.92\% success on RoboDojo and 76.0\% on RoboTwin 2.0-our analysis reveals a pronounced gap between semantic reasoning and physical execution, particularly in consequence-aware action planning, precision, and complex motion coordination. To further examine these limitations, we introduce LIBERO-GeoMotion, a new benchmark of geometry-constrained tasks that require precise pose alignment, coordinated translation and rotation, and anticipation of physical action consequences. GPT-6 Astra achieves only 11.1\% zero-shot success, exposing the difficulty of translating spatial understanding into physically feasible motion. Real-world experiments corroborate these findings: zero-shot execution is feasible for simple tasks, yet persistent deficits remain in motion feasibility, precise control, and physical safety, while substantial inference latency further hinders practical deployment. Overall, our results characterize the emerging embodied capabilities of general-purpose multimodal models and delineate the key challenges toward safe, efficient, and reliable robotic manipulation.

deep_dive.title: Near-Optimal Consistency-Robustness Bounds for Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling
deep_dive.abstract: We study the problem of characterizing the optimal consistency--robustness tradeoff for single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predicted processing times. For a fixed number of jobs $n$, Wei and Zhang (2020) established a lower bound on the achievable consistency--robustness tradeoff which is known to be tight only in a few restrictive cases, leaving the optimal tradeoff for general $n$ unresolved. A different worst-case-$n$ regime was introduced by Benomar et al. (2025), who applied the former work's construction to show that for $λ\in (0, 1)$, any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must be $1 + Ω(\sqrt{1/λ})$-robust. On the other hand, the best known upper bound gives $(1+λ)$-consistency and $1+O(1/λ)$-robustness, leaving a polynomial gap. In this work, we develop a new lower bound using a multi-stage adversarial construction and a new algorithm that together give a near-optimal characterization of the consistency--robustness tradeoff: for every $n$, our upper bound is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of our lower bound, and thus our algorithm is within a multiplicative factor $3/2$ of the online optimal. In particular, our lower bound shows that any $(1+λ)$-consistent algorithm must have robustness at least $1/\sqrtλ$ as $n \to \infty$, while our algorithm achieves robustness at most $\frac{1}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}+1/λ}$ for any $n$, matching the lower bound in the leading term as $λ\downarrow 0$; our upper bound also closes the polynomial gap in the worst-case-$n$ regime. We additionally show how our algorithm can be made error-tolerant, preserving the near-optimal consistency-robustness tradeoff while incurring only slightly degraded performance under bounded prediction errors.

deep_dive.title: Hard and Soft Real-Time DNN Inference Scheduling on Heterogeneous Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning
deep_dive.abstract: We present a scheduling framework for heterogeneous multi-accelerator systems executing both hard real-time and soft real-time QoS-aware DNN inference workloads. The framework combines an online reinforcement learning (RL) scheduler with a deterministic runtime safety layer. The RL scheduler dynamically generates candidate schedules by jointly selecting sub-job priorities and accelerator assignments, while runtime certification guarantees that all HRT deadlines remain satisfied independently of the learned policy.   To enable runtime certification in heterogeneous precedence-constrained systems, we introduce a schedulability-preserving prefix replacement criterion based on machine-wise cuts. The proposed criterion guarantees that runtime-generated schedule prefixes preserve the existence of a feasible continuation without requiring complete finish-time dominance with respect to a feasible reference schedule.   Experimental results on heterogeneous DNN accelerator platforms show that the proposed framework preserves HRT schedulability while improving QoS-aware deadline satisfaction, client-level service quality, and accelerator utilization compared to state-of-the-art scheduling approaches.

deep_dive.title: An Introduction to World Models for Generalist Agents
deep_dive.abstract: World models have recently emerged as a promising direction toward developing generalist agents capable of understanding, predicting, and interacting with diverse environments. However, despite growing interest, the concept of a world model remains loosely defined, encompassing approaches ranging from predictive dynamics models and learned simulators to models that jointly generate future observations and actions. This introductory paper aims to clarify the concept of world models and provide a unified perspective on their role in developing generalist agents. Starting from the partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) framework, we connect world modeling to classical control, dynamical systems, signal processing, and reinforcement learning. We introduce different approaches to world modeling, emphasizing the knowledge they capture, their learning objectives, and how they support decision-making. We further explore the relationship between world modeling and policy learning, highlighting how these capabilities can be unified through conditional prediction without requiring separate models. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey of existing methods, this paper focuses on fundamental concepts, modeling principles, and connections, with the goal of providing an accessible and unified introduction to world models for generalist agents.

deep_dive.title: BOLT: Multi-Bottleneck Bound-Guided Learning for Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling with Time Lags and Resource-Coupled Transport
deep_dive.abstract: Flexible job-shop scheduling becomes resource-coupled when a scarce vehicle fleet moves jobs between stations, because the schedule sets the transport waits. BOLT (bound-oriented learning for transport-coupled scheduling) builds a lower bound from chain, machine-capacity, and fleet-capacity relaxations. The bound equals the makespan at termination, so its per-step changes form a reward that sums to a constant minus the makespan. Because it never exceeds the attainable makespan, each candidate's bound increase is a proven rise of the makespan floor, which the policy reads as a price. The root bound certifies a completed schedule's suboptimality gap without a solver. On industry-motivated 10-module prefabricated-construction instances, explicit transport coupling outperforms a transport-penalty policy in every tested cell where loaded moves occupy at least 66% of fleet time and in none at or below 56%. Across five zero-shot 50- and 80-module production batches, BOLT outperforms the best dispatching-rule pair on four and the penalty policy on the three with long moves. In the three-vehicle 80-module batch, its mean makespan is 13.0% below the best pair and 4.2% below an hour-budget constraint-programming solver whose proven gap averages 34%. BOLT decides in 2.3-5.9 ms per event on one processor core and re-plans a disruption in seconds.

quick_skim.title: Communication-Free Distributed Multi-Robot Task Allocation under Partial Observations Using Labeled Multi-Bernoulli Filtering
quick_skim.abstract: This paper proposes a communication-free multi-robot task allocation framework based solely on local observations. In this study, tasks are defined as reaching target locations. Each robot estimates the positions of neighboring robots using a Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (LMB) filter and independently assigns tasks through a greedy auction-based strategy. By continuously updating state estimates and reallocating tasks during execution, the proposed method enables decentralized coordination without explicit communication. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that the proposed method enables effective cooperative task allocation without inter-robot communication while remaining robust to measurement clutter and observation uncertainty.

quick_skim.title: Dynamic Load Balancing under Restricting Updates
quick_skim.abstract: We study the problem of load balancing in the dynamic setting. The input is a bipartite graph $G = (J \cup M, E)$ of jobs $J$ and machines $M$. Every job has a positive weight $w(j)$. The goal is to assign every job in $J$ to an adjacent machine in $M$ so as to minimize the maximum machine load, where the load of a machine is the sum of the weights of the jobs assigned to it.   Although load balancing has been studied extensively in many models of computation, the only previous result in the dynamic model addresses the \emph{incremental} setting, where updates take the form of edge insertions and job deletions [BKS23b]. The authors show a $(1+ε)$-approximation for incremental \emph{fractional} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/ε)$ update time; they point out that their techniques do not extend to the decremental setting.   Main Result: We obtain an algorithm which maintains a $(1+ε)$-approximate solution to the fractional load balancing problem under edge deletions and job insertions in $\tilde{O}(\log (n), 1/ε)$ update time. Our techniques are very different from those of the incremental algorithm of [BKS23b]. Instead, our algorithm is inspired by a load-balancing algorithm from the {\sc congest} model of computation [ALPZ21]. We develop a novel analytic framework for this algorithm, which allows us to show that it performs well in the dynamic setting.   Rounding Scheme: We also present a black-box rounding scheme for dynamic load balancing. Plugging in our fractional algorithm, we obtain a decremental algorithm for $(2+ε)$-approximate \emph{integral} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/ε)$ update time. We also obtain the same bounds for incremental load balancing by plugging in the fractional algorithm of [BKS23b].

quick_skim.title: Fault-Tolerant Offloading Framework for Real-Time Applications in Mobile Edge Computing
quick_skim.abstract: This paper studies a Deadline-constrained task Offloading and resource Allocation Problem (DOAP) in a backhaul-network-enabled Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) system with both bandwidth and computational resource constraints. The goal is to maximize the total inference accuracy improvement across all tasks. We formulate this problem, denoted as $\mathbf{P}$, as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem and show it is NP-hard via a reduction from the maximum-weight three-dimensional matching problem. To address $\mathbf{P}$, we develop $\mathtt{FastSA}$, a linear-time $\frac{1}{10}$-approximation algorithm based on the local-ratio technique. To the best of our knowledge, $\mathtt{FastSA}$ provides the first constant-factor performance guarantee for backhaul-network-enabled DOAPs. In addition, we introduce a fault detection and recovery framework that enables robust MEC operation under backhaul link and edge server failures. Experiments using profiled image classification workloads and real-world taxi traces show that $\mathtt{FastSA}$ achieves an average accuracy improvement of $25.6\%$ over benchmark algorithms under fault-free conditions while maintaining the lowest runtime. Under fault-injected scenarios, our framework reduces performance degradation by an average of $12.8\%$, demonstrating its effectiveness in fault handling.

quick_skim.title: Aging-Aware Online Distributed Scheduling for Lifecycle Carbon Reduction in Geo-Distributed Data Centers
quick_skim.abstract: The rapid proliferation of data centers (DCs), driven by cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI), has led to massive energy demand and carbon emissions, posing significant sustainability challenges. Carbon-aware optimization in geographically distributed data centers has been widely studied. Most existing approaches mainly focus on operational carbon emissions from server usage. However, existing literature often ignores workload-induced thermal stress, which accelerates nonlinear hardware degradation. This leads to more frequent server replacements and ultimately increases embodied carbon emissions. To address these limitations, we propose a comprehensive carbon life-cycle modeling framework for distributed data centers. Apart from operational carbon emissions, this work combines workload scheduling with a utilization-dependent exponential aging model to evaluate long-term carbon costs from server degradation. In order to solve the proposed optimization model in an online and privacy-preserving manner, an enhanced Lyapunov framework with time-varying queue shifting (TVQS) is first introduced to handle system uncertainties. Then, a zero-sum perturbation-based alternating direction method of multipliers (ZSP-ADMM) framework is developed to enable distributed coordination across geographically separated data centers while protecting locally exchanged workload information. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 13.0% lower carbon emissions and 12.6% lower operational costs compared with benchmarks.

quick_skim.title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning
quick_skim.abstract: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.

quick_skim.title: Joint Freshness and Deadline Feasibility in Store-and-Forward Satellite IoT Networks
quick_skim.abstract: 3GPP Release 19 supports store-and-forward satel- lite access, where traffic accumulated during feeder-link outages must be forwarded through finite, geometry-limited windows. Static priority levels offer little discrimination among large backlogs and ignore the decay in packet value. We formulate QoS feasibility for status updates, measured by destination freshness, and deadline-constrained event reports over periodic two-hop contacts with finite onboard storage. For general calendars, we derive ordering-sensitive miss, cohort-capacity, delivery-rate, and freshness bounds, including an exact status-only characterization. For single status flow and single event class sharing a contact pair per period, a finite-state program gives exact joint feasibility for arbitrary integer age thresholds. Numerical results quantify tradeoffs among load, capacity, deadline, and freshness tolerance.

quick_skim.title: Robust Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling with Classification Models
quick_skim.abstract: We study the classical single-machine scheduling problem of minimizing the sum of completion times of jobs in a non-clairvoyant setting, where the processing time of each job remains unknown until its completion. This is a hard problem for which no constant competitive algorithm is possible. Inspired by robust optimization and learning-augmented algorithms, we introduce a novel robustness framework that leverages structural information provided by a classification model to overcome this limitation. Specifically, we assume that jobs are partitioned into classes and we have access to the confusion matrix of the classifier, whose entry $(k,\ell)$ indicates the number of jobs predicted to belong to class~$k$ but that actually belong to class~$\ell$. In this manner, we are able to characterize uncertainty as a set of permutations within each predicted class, rather than as a collection of discrete numerical scenarios, avoiding the computational difficulty of classical robust metrics, such as Min-Max and Min-Max Regret. In addition to these worst-case metrics, we also consider the expected objective over all scenarios. We first propose an optimal non-adaptive strategy that is oblivious with respect to all three robust criteria. We then investigate adaptive and randomized algorithms, showing that they can outperform the optimal non-adaptive strategy when the matrix exhibits particular structural properties.

quick_skim.title: CoRS: Fast Neural Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling via Composite Interval State Reuse
quick_skim.abstract: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) typically refresh graph representations and update feasibility after every operation--machine decision. However, only feasibility must remain exact at every step, whereas graph encoding is substantially more expensive and can potentially be refreshed less frequently. We present CoRS, which decouples them: an interval-level graph representation is reused across multiple sequential decisions, while a stepwise feasibility state is updated after every action. This two-timescale design amortizes graph encoding without parallelizing action generation or relaxing scheduling constraints. CoRS further develops a feasibility-preserving composite-interval decoding scheme with dynamic constraint tracking and boundary state synchronization, which reduces representation refresh frequency while maintaining continuous feasible schedule construction. Furthermore, to alleviate representation staleness caused by interval-level state reuse, CoRS introduces enhanced static features as a compensation mechanism. By providing more comprehensive structural information of the scheduling problem, these features improve the model's perception of overall problem characteristics. Extensive experiments on synthetic and multiple public FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that CoRS significantly reduces inference time while maintaining competitive solution quality, achieving favorable speed-quality trade-offs under tight wall-clock budgets and low-latency scenarios.

quick_skim.title: Tight Bounds for Paging with Time Windows and Joint Replenishment with Varying Opening Costs
quick_skim.abstract: We study the paging with time windows problem, a natural generalization of classical paging, in which each request must be served within a specified time interval. This model allows the algorithm to delay service and batch service requests over time, but also introduces significant challenges due to overlapping requests. While the problem is well understood in the unweighted setting, where optimal $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithms are known, the weighted case remains more elusive. The best previously known algorithm, due to Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi, achieves an $O(\log k \log n)$-competitive ratio, leaving a gap between weighted and unweighted settings.   We obtain an $O(\log k)$-competitive algorithm for weighted paging with time windows, matching the optimal competitive ratio. The core of our approach is a structural decomposition that separates the evolution of the cache from the scheduling of page loads. We show that, given a sequence of cache configurations, computing a near-optimal sequence of page loads reduces to a variant of the Joint Replenishment Problem with deadlines (JRP-D) with time-dependent opening costs. We design a constant-competitive online algorithm for this variant and prove that the reduction is tight. Combining this with an existing online construction of cache configurations yields the desired bound.

quick_skim.title: TRACE: Tackling Real-World Resource Assignment Problems via Agentic Heuristic Design
quick_skim.abstract: Dynamic resource assignment, the real-time allocation of task streams to heterogeneous processing nodes, is the backbone of modern computing infrastructure. While learning-based schedulers excel in research, industrial deployments still rely on hand-written rules that operators can read, audit, and execute within tight latency budgets. LLM-based Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) promises to automate writing such rules. However, existing AHD frameworks were developed for combinatorial problems fully specified to the LLM, and they learn only from a scalar fitness score. In real systems, the behaviour that determines a good heuristic, such as processor speeds or power consumption, is unknown a priori: the score reveals which heuristic performs better, but not why. This missing information is recorded in the system logs that every evaluation produces. Exploiting it is non-trivial: logs are massive and noisy, the relevant signals depend on the objective, and their content and format vary across hardware and software stacks, so they can neither be fed to an LLM as is nor processed by a fixed parser. We propose TRACE, which couples an evolutionary AHD loop with an agentic knowledge-extraction workflow. A Reasoner agent analyzes the log schema in light of the objective and formulates hypotheses about the system dynamics; a Coder agent writes and executes schema-specific code to test them, producing insights or executable tools for the evolved heuristics. We evaluate TRACE on a synthetic cloud benchmark and a 5G vRAN scenario built from industrial testbed measurements and operational traffic traces. TRACE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art AHD methods in resource assignment problems and yields more auditable heuristics at under 2% overhead.

quick_skim.title: CQTwin: A Digital-Twin Toolkit for Operational Analytics of HPC Schedulers
quick_skim.abstract: HPC facilities collect years of job scheduler records, yet much of this operational data remains underused because accessible tools for turning it into actionable insight are scarce. We present CQTwin, an open-source digital-twin toolkit for operational analytics of HPC scheduling data. CQTwin addresses this gap through two complementary modes: offline trace replay and online event-driven simulation. Built on the Python-based CQSim discrete-event simulator, CQTwin combines a fidelity-validated, high-performance C++ engine with an interactive browser-based dashboard and a Snapshot Lab, enabling facility staff, operators, and researchers to characterize workloads, compare scheduling policies, and explore what-if scenarios. As an offline twin, CQTwin replays archived workload traces under alternative policies to show how the same workload would have unfolded under different scheduling decisions. As an online twin, it consumes job events as they arrive and projects how alternative policies would process the currently queued jobs, providing guidance for real-time decision-making. The dashboard supports the complete analysis workflow, including workload characterization, experiment configuration and monitoring, and multidimensional comparison of simulation results, allowing users to determine visually which policies best suit a workload and what trade-offs they entail. We validate CQTwin using production traces from the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility spanning 2016-2023.

quick_skim.title: Adaptive Deadline- and Energy-Aware Caching Algorithms in Dynamic Multi-UAV Edge Networks
quick_skim.abstract: Content caching via unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) becomes one of the solutions to maintain content delivery when terrestrial infrastructure is unavailable or disrupted. However, existing caching approaches often focus primarily on cache-hit performance or average delivery delay, without jointly addressing spatially heterogeneous and time-varying demand, content-specific deadlines, and uneven communication-energy consumption across UAVs. To address these challenges, we formulate a dynamic deadline- and energy-aware cache placement and replacement problem that jointly considers deadline misses, UAV-side communication energy, and inter-UAV energy imbalance. To achieve this, we first develop deadline- and energy-aware UBAC (DE-UBAC), an interpretable hierarchical rule-based realization that incorporates deadline-aware prioritization, cooperative placement, energy-aware coordination, and cache-update cost. However, predefined priorities and thresholds limit its adaptability under dynamically coupled network conditions. We therefore propose GRU-assisted Deadline- and Energy-aware Proximal Policy Optimization (GRU-DEPPO), which combines local and global GRU-based temporal representations with a centralized PPO actor-critic for adaptive cache placement and replacement. Simulation results show that GRU-DEPPO achieves the lowest deadline-miss rate and total UAV-side communication energy among the considered schemes. Compared with DE-UBAC, GRU-DEPPO reduces the deadline-miss rate by approximately 61% and inter-UAV energy imbalance by approximately 40%.
